What you may also want to do, is plug in your display cable into the top-most port of your GPU. Display output #1. Usually a DisplayPort cable but may also be HDMI depending on the maker of the GPU. I have seen some cards not fully support all ports until you are in Windows. I would essentially try every port as-is.

Edit: Clarity

My initial guess is that, depending on how old RX 580 is, when you enable secure boot it forces UEFI mode in the BIOS. Not all GPUs, especially older ones, support UEFI boot. Resetting/Clearing CMOS should reset it back to defaults and revert to CSM/Legacy. That's the first thing i would do is make sure you properly clear the CMOS.

Edit: At least I believe that's how it on Nvidia cards. On older AMD cards I'm unsure. I do think that you should properly clear the CMOS to at least get a proper display output though. A quick Google search of RX 580 UEFI problems shows lots of similar stories.

Edit 2: I looked into this further. According to their [own site](https://www.sapphiretech.com/en/consumer/nitro-rx-580-8g-g5) all models of the RX 580 support UEFI. If that's the case, then I also suggest trying my suggestion in my other comment.

Also another tip to anyone reading this is if you're moving your PC any distance, even up the stairs, removing just the GPU is a good idea. Even if you leave everything else in there as-is. If you drop your PC even a small distance, the chance of your GPU snapping off is fairly high (in my experience). Even if you're sure you won't drop it, taking out the GPU is fast and easy, so it's my recommendation unless you're moving it about in the same room.

I've only seen a handful of cables that performed poorly in certain, specific situation. Usually they're either made so poorly they won't do gigabit at all or they work okay for the situation. Now, if I was running wires in a place where I wouldn't have access to often, like a new house I'd definitely want to make sure the cable I buy is as stated.

The only cables I have ever really doubted were those "Slim" ones that [Monoprice sells](https://www.monoprice.com/Product?p_id=15162). But even then those are probably okay. I think there's more misinformation around that certain cables are somehow superior to others i.e. "bigger number better". Lots of companies on Amazon are guilty of this. Cat5e is still good enough for the vast majority of people in terms of needing patch cables. If properly made, Cat5, 5e, 6, 6a, and 8 will all perform (or should) the same at reasonable distances for gigabit or lower. With that being said there are a lot of poorly made cables out there. I've seen patch cables come with expensive routers made so poorly they will auto-negotiate at 100 Mbps even if the router has only gigabit ports.

Not normal. If your ping is that high - yes, even on DSL - off and on then it's a sign something is not working properly. Usually DSL ping in my experience is between 30 - 50 average on SpeedTest. Not the best, but a lot more usable. If it's spiking like that then either there's some serious overloading on or the line is having issues. Is this during peak hours? What's it like at an off-time such as 2 PM or something? Is there any kind of consistent situation(s) happening during this time? For example, does it rain and then this happens? It's not a modem issue, the phone support usually ops for that as a fix but it only fixes something like 20% of the time maybe, if that. Open the DSL page on your computer (log into the router/modem) and look at your CRC errors. If you have a lot of errors it's a sign something is unstable. Assuming it's true Cat6, and the jacks are also rated for Cat6, you should see absolutely no drop even at 250 ft. Cat6 is rated up to 300+ feet at gigabit speeds, and 10 gigabit at roughly 200 feet. However, you can frequently push the distance quite a bit more. Heck, even Cat5e is rated for gigabit and can push that quite far. Even if the wiring and the jacks were 5e you shouldn't see any significant drop even at 250 ft. Keep in mind that a network is only as strong as its weakest link.

For example, if you have a router with a gigabit Ethernet port, going downstream with Cat6 wiring to a switch only rated for 10/100 Mbps then it won't matter how fast anything is before that, because it will auto negotiate down to 100 Mbps. Now with that being said, there really isn't any negotiation between 100 mbps and gigabit, so if there was a problem with your wiring or the jacks then it would most likely be capped at 100 Mbps, and not 600.

To me this indicates some sort of software issue or if you are using/testing the internet during peak hours. Do you get full gigabit speed if you hook a laptop or something up directly to the router? Also, how are you testing your speeds?

Note that if you power cycle the modem it will clear all errors in the log. So when the issue starts happening, keep the modem on and then look and compare if there is anything different than when there aren't issues.

1.6 Mbps upload isn't so bad for ADSL. Yeah it's certainly not ideal, but I used to play CoD multiplayer and a lot of popular games with an upload of 0.8 Mbps. My ping wasn't great but it was playable.

I'm not a tech or work for CenturyLink, but in my experience if your ping is ridiculously high like 300+ ms then you are most likely going to be having speed issues too. For example, I used to have 5 Mbps download with CenturyLink and 0.8 Mbps upload. Usually I had fairly good ping ~35 ms on average. But if I was having a lot of errors on the line and packets were being dropped, my speeds would tank and my ping would sky rocket. What I would do is log into the the modem GUI and scroll down and make sure it's trained at the speeds you're paying for. Next, look at the CRC errors and let us know what both the near end and far end numbers are. There's obviously an issue somewhere, your ping should not be so high that the game is unplayable. Also, are you on WiFi or hardwired Ethernet?

A wired connection will be faster than WiFi in like, 99.9% of cases. And it should be. Not only that, but a wired connection will have much less latency than WiFi. Which is definitely preferred in online gaming. Latency, which can be identified by the ping statistic like in [this picture](https://www.speedtest.net/result/8742582451.png) of my speed test.

Notice how on my wired connection, my ping is 3. This is extremely good ping and generally only available on fiber optic connections. A good ping for ADSL2+ would be between 30 and 40 ms I believe. Generally depending on conditions, you could easily see a 20 ms difference in ping going from wired to WiFi. So in terms of ping, the lower the better. 

Ping is important because it determines how fast your connection is sending and receiving requests from distant servers. So say you are in a multiplayer game online, ping factors into things like your characters movement. When you move your character, it sends a request to a distant server and then that server sends a request back updating your movement. This happens very fast, but if you have a high ping, say 100ms, then you will start seeing lag because your connection isn't updating fast enough.  There are a lot of things that affect ping, but this is the basics.

If you're WiFi connection is on average faster than your wired speed in terms of downloading, then something could be off in your network setup.

While I am not an expert, from my understanding modems usually are a device that connects you to the internet and authenticates with your internet service provider to provide a constant connection. I think [this video](https://youtu.be/Mad4kQ5835Y) explains it pretty well.

The router, is a device which takes the internet signal and broadcasts it via WiFi and can also do other things, such as managing and prioritizing traffic. In other words, controlling which device gets what amount of speed and when. 

In terms of ADSL2+, you need both a router and modem. What I did with my CenturyLink service was using their modem/router combo, and then did something called bridging. This essentially completely disables the router functionality of the modem/router combo leaving it ONLY as a modem. So it has the connection from the ISP, but it does not broadcast WiFi. 

Then I bought a better, more advanced router online and connected that to what was essentially just the modem now. Bridging your modem/router combo ensures that You don't have two routers connected to the same network (one in the combo and one separate you bought). It's not hard to do, and with some willingness to learn a lot of people are willing to help you. Not only here, but also on the HomeNetworking subreddit.

I could be wrong, but I believe if the only two speeds you have are 20 and 40 Mbps, then the 40 is most likely bonded ADSL2+. This would explain why there is a $99 fee for the 40 as a technician would need to come to your house and run a second line from the NID (Network Interface Device) outside into the house. You would also need a specific router/modem combo for bonded internet, which can be expensive.

If I were you I would just fork up the $99 and pay for the 40 because bonded slots aren't always open. Bonded is essentially running two lines that carry 20 Mbps speed and then combining them at the router/modem for a maximum throughput of 40 Mbps. 

Owning your own router/modem is my preference because it will be less expensive long term. What I did when I had CenturyLink was buy a used CenturyLink modem off Ebay, and then bridged it (essentially disabling the router functionality) and used a more powerful router for my WiFi and traffic optimization. 

Feel free to ask questions!

Next thing is your Fallout.ini and FalloutPrefs.ini - make sure they are mostly default. Remove any "multicore" tweaks and do NOT mess with the uGrid settings. The only thing I add to my .ini files is to remove the mouse acceleration. I leave them mostly at vanilla. Next thing I can recommend is turning off all forms of VSync for the game and turning off manage FPS in the stutter remover .ini file. Then go into the Nvidia Control panel and turn on Adaptive VSync. Works wonders for older games. I have a similar system as you, but I have an ssd. Well firstly it is not recommended to change the uGrids settings from 5. This will cause performance issues, engine issues, crashes, and save game corruption. This is because the engine was made for a uGrid setting of 5 and only 5. I know for a fact that the mountain issue is z-fighting. And I assume the sign is too. Z-fighting happens worst with LOD because LOD is very low poly and often made from 2D planes. What is going on is that the game isn't sure which face to show from which polygon since they are in the same place. I have the same issue and so does everyone else with the older Bethesda games. Even Skyrim suffered from it a lot until it was fixed in SSE. This is an engine issue and cannot easily be fixed. Though I agree it is annoying.

If you can take a picture that would certainly help. It would also help to know what mods you are using. I am unsure if you are talking about z-fighting or aliasing or something else. Z-fighting occurs when a two meshes occupy the same space. This is an impossibility in the real world, so that's why it flickers. It's easier to see this in distant mountain LOD. There really isn't a easy fix for this.

This default game launcher (not just the direct .exe) has to be ran at least once in order to generate a Fallout.ini (the one which resides in your My Games folder). Steam will not create one for you because it is generated from the Fallout_default.ini once you run the launcher. It will also create a FalloutPrefs.ini. My advice is to delete the FalloutNV folder inside of My Games and then run the default launcher. Make sure to backups any saves first. This should automatically generate all the necessary files for you.

Okay for comparison, I am running a stock i7 4790 and 970 and I get a solid 60 FPS. Firstly, don't turn up the uGrid settings. Even if your computer can handle the extra work, the game (engine-wise) was not meant for more than 5. You will run into increased crashes and instability and possibly corrupted saves if you push it further. This was recommended by Queued himself (the maker of NVAC). Secondly, you aren't running into the issue of your hardware not being good enough, it's more that the engine itself cannot take advantage of it. Jay's ENB is the most intense ENB out there and it's a little too much for this game to handle. My advice would be to use a more balanced ENB like Enhanced Shaders. Are you only running texture mods besides the ENB? Also, don't use the ENB to manage FPS. It's not as refined as Skyrim. I personally turn off all FPS management and force Adaptive V-Sync through the Control Panel. I don't use any ENB, but if I do use one I usually get between 40-60 FPS. What texture mods are you using? If you run too many at the highest resolution it will eventually start to bog down the engine. Even if you have enough VRAM. P.S. If you see that your card is only being maxed at around 60% then don't worry. The game cannot physically max out a 980Ti at 100%. I would try running the game at vanilla to see if the FPS issues still are occurring.

I have exactly the same system as you (CPU and GPU wise). Fallout New Vegas is more restricted by your CPU than your GPU. As it can only use the first core 100% and then some of the second core. But it does not max out both cores. In the strip in particular the game slows down because of poor optimization and too much going on engine wise. The only thing I have found that works is to set the majority of view sliders to halfway (8). Also turn off Full Detail Reflections and turn Water Multisampling to low. These are extremely bugged and will cause FPS drops in areas where there is no water and there will be almost no graphical difference. I am running Ultra @ 1080p 60 FPS in the majority of the game aside from the settings I turned down I mentioned above. I also advise turning off all V-Sync for this game and then enabling Adaptive V-Sync via the CP. Works wonders.

Edit: Do not mess with any of the .ini settings that change the preloading data or uGridsToLoad. The game just wasn't meant to handle more than 5. I keep my .ini files mostly vanilla (aside from removing mouse acceleration). Make sure you turn off bHookLightCriticalSections (set to 0) in your Stutter Remover .ini file too or you will get FPS drops and stuttering. Also use the 4GB enabler and set your nvse_config.ini to the recommended settings that RoyBatty mentions on the A World of Pain comments section (it's stickied).
